about: WHO IMCI distance learning course (2014), Module 1, in the Sudan national IMNCI wording. Each WHO section is cut into short lessons of one topic, with the same information as the WHO module, laid out as activities: step-by-step cards, flip cards, sorting, case stories and questions. Where the Sudan national booklet differs from WHO, the Sudan wording is used and a "Sudan national protocol" note says what WHO wrote. Chart booklet and recording form blocks are read live from the protocol. Video slots without a link show a placeholder; their narration scripts are in a separate file. Exercises start as drafts and open in the exercise manager.

read.text: See what Module 1 covers and where it fits in the IMCI process, then take the pre-test.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text:
During the first face-to-face meeting you learned that the IMCI process always begins by checking all children for signs of serious illness.

In the sick child aged 2 months up to 5 years these are called general danger signs. In this module you will learn about these signs.
A sick child is 2 months up to 5 years of age. This means the child has not had his 5th birthday.
read.label: Key point

read.text: Note that the signs of serious illness for the sick young infant (under 2 months of age) are called general danger signs of serious disease. In Module 2 you will learn more about these signs and care for the sick young infant.
What you will be able to do

After you study this module, you will know how to:

  • Greet a caregiver and get important information for IMCI
  • Recognize general danger signs in a sick child
  • Provide urgent pre-referral treatment according to IMCI instructions
  • Refer a child when danger signs are present
How the module is organized

This module is divided into the following sections:

  1. Greet the caregiver
  2. Check for general danger signs
  3. Care when urgent referral is required
Where does this module fit in the IMCI process?
This module focuses on the first two steps in the IMCI process: greeting the caregiver and checking for general danger signs.

read.title: The IMCI process for every sick child

steps.title: Greet the caregiver
steps.text: Ask about the child's problems. This module.

steps.title: Check for general danger signs
steps.text: Check every sick child. If one or more signs are present, the child requires urgent referral: continue the assessment quickly so that referral is not delayed. This module.

steps.title: Continue the assessment
steps.text: Assess for main symptoms (cough or difficult breathing, diarrhoea, fever, ear problems), check for malnutrition and anaemia, check immunization status, HIV status and other problems. Modules 3 to 9.

read.text: Greet a caregiver well, use five good communication skills, and find out the four things you need before you assess.
read.label: In this lesson

read.title: Checking all sick children for general danger signs
read.caption: Watch this first. It walks through the whole section.

read.text: You will begin with a case study. This scene should be similar to situations that you see in your clinic. After it, you will learn how to (a) greet the caregiver and get important information about the child, and (b) check for general danger signs.

stages.text: Lebo's grandmother carries him into the clinic. Lebo does not look well. She has walked for one hour to the clinic. She tells you that she is also taking care of 4 other grandchildren. Lebo is her youngest grandchild and she is very worried about him. She says he is acting very unwell and has had a cough for 7 days.

The grandmother tells you as she sits down that Lebo's mother died 2 months ago. She says she does not know what caused the mother to die. Lebo's father works away and does not come home, only once every year or so. The grandmother is very worried about Lebo and very tired from her walking.

She tells you this is the first time she is bringing Lebo in to the clinic. You ask her how old Lebo is. She says he is 19 months old. You ask Lebo's grandmother her name. She tells you that her name is Nthabeleng.
stages.question: What is the first thing you do when Nthabeleng comes to the clinic?
options: Greet the caregiver and ask about the child
Take Lebo's temperature straight away
Refer Lebo to hospital at once
stages.explanation: The first step in the IMCI process is to greet the caregiver and ask about the child.

read.text: Why greet the caregiver?

Greeting the caregiver has two purposes:

  1. It makes a caregiver feel welcome in the clinic. Greeting and welcoming a caregiver is an important first step in building trust. It begins good and caring communication.
  2. It helps you gather important information about why the child is coming to the clinic.
Why is good communication with a caregiver important?

Caregivers can be very stressed and emotional when a child is ill. It is important for health workers to communicate concern and care for the child's health, and the family's situation. Good communication helps to reassure the caregiver that her child will receive good care.

When you treat the child's illness later in the visit, you will need to teach and advise the caregiver about caring for her sick child at home. Good communication and trust is essential here. It is important to have good communication with the caregiver from the beginning of the visit.

cards.back: Listen carefully to what the caregiver tells you. This shows you are taking her concerns seriously.
Use words the caregiver understands. If she does not understand what you ask her, she cannot give the information you need to assess and classify the child correctly.
Give the caregiver time to answer the questions. She might need time to decide if a sign you are asking about is present.
Ask additional questions when the caregiver is not sure about her answer. If she is not sure that a certain symptom or sign is present, ask additional questions. Help her make her answers clearer.
Praise the caregiver for what she is doing right. This will reinforce good practices.

read.text: What information do you gather during a greeting?
When you greet a caregiver you begin to ask important information about the child. This will help you in your assessment.

cards.back: The child's age determines which IMCI charts to use: the sick child or the young infant.

Why is the caregiver bringing the child to the clinic? Note the symptoms or health problems that are worrying them. If necessary, ask further detail: for example, how long the symptom has been present, or if it has been getting worse. You can also ask how she has been addressing the problem so far: this gives you background about previous care in the home, community, or other facilities.

Check if they are already recorded on the child's card. If not, weigh the child and measure his temperature later when you assess and classify the child's main symptoms. Do not undress or disturb the child now.
Is this the first visit for this problem, or a follow-up visit? These visits are different, so this is another important piece of information.

read.text:
ASK: first time coming to the clinic for this problem?

YES: INITIAL VISIT
ASSESS and CLASSIFY according to IMCI		NO: FOLLOW-UP VISIT
Give follow-up care according to IMCI

This is an initial visit if it is the child's first for this episode of illness. It is a follow-up visit if the child was seen a few days ago for the same problem. You will learn more about follow-up visits in later modules.

stages.text: Nthabeleng said that Lebo is 19 months old.
stages.question: Which charts will you use for Lebo?
options: The sick child charts
The young infant charts
stages.explanation: Lebo is 19 months old: 2 months up to 5 years is a sick child.

stages.text: Nthabeleng tells you that Lebo has had a cough for 7 days. She also says that he has not been eating well. Nthabeleng is very worried about this. She says that in the past two days, he cannot take anything at all and she says he is very weak. This is concerning to you.
stages.question: Is Lebo coming for an initial or a follow-up visit?
options: An initial visit
A follow-up visit
stages.explanation: Nthabeleng told you that this is her first time bringing him to the clinic for this issue.

stages.text: Lebo's temperature and weight were recorded when he came into the clinic: he weighs 10 kg and his temperature is 37 °C. You can now fill in the top of Lebo's recording form.

Check every sick child for the general danger signs, one at a time, and say what you do when you find one.

Before you start
read.text: A child sleeps on her mother's lap. Is she lethargic?
options: Yes
Not necessarily: wake her and look
No, sleeping children are never sick
feedback: Sleeping is not the same as lethargic.
Right. Look at how she wakes and responds.
A sleeping child can be lethargic. You must look.

read.text: After greeting the caregiver, how do you begin assessing the child?

The first thing you check every sick child for is general danger signs. These signs are critically important. If Lebo shows any one of these signs, he is in danger. He needs urgent pre-referral treatment and immediate referral to the hospital.

A general danger sign is present if:

  • the child is not able to drink or breastfeed
  • the child vomits everything
  • the child has had more than one convulsion or prolonged convulsions, or is convulsing
  • the child is lethargic or unconscious
How will you check for a general danger sign?
You will ASK three questions and LOOK at the child. Open your chart booklet to the chart for general danger signs; it is shown here from the national protocol.

read.caption: Chart booklet: check for general danger signs (Sudan national IMNCI booklet)

read.title: Checking for general danger signs, one step at a time

steps.title: ASK: Is the child able to drink or breastfeed?
steps.text: A child has the sign not able to drink or breastfeed if the child is not able to suck or swallow when offered a drink or breast milk. Make sure the caregiver understands the question. If she says the child is not able to drink or breastfeed, ask her to describe what happens when she offers the child something to drink: is the child able to take fluid into his mouth and swallow it? If you are not sure about her answer, ask her to offer the child a drink of clean water or breast milk, and look to see if the child swallows. A breastfed child may have difficulty sucking when his nose is blocked: clear it. If the child can breastfeed after the nose is cleared, the child does not have this danger sign.

steps.title: ASK: Does the child vomit everything?
steps.text: A child who is not able to hold anything down at all has the sign vomits everything: everything that goes down comes back up. He will not be able to hold down food, fluids, or oral drugs. A child who vomits several times but can hold down some fluids does not have this sign. Use words the caregiver understands and give her time to answer. If she is not sure, ask how often the child vomits, and whether he vomits each time he swallows food or fluids. If you are still not sure, ask her to offer the child a drink and see if he vomits.

steps.title: ASK: Has the child had convulsions?
steps.text: Ask if the child has had more than one convulsion, or prolonged convulsions, during this current illness. During a convulsion, the child's arms and legs stiffen because the muscles are contracting. The child may lose consciousness or not be able to respond to spoken directions. Use words the caregiver understands: she may call convulsions "fits" or "spasms".

steps.title: LOOK: Is the child lethargic or unconscious?
steps.text: A lethargic child is not awake and alert when she should be. She is drowsy and does not show interest in what is happening around her. Often the lethargic child does not look at the caregiver or watch your face when you talk, or will not respond if you clap or snap your fingers. The child may stare blankly. An unconscious child cannot be wakened: he does not respond when touched, shaken, or spoken to. Ask the caregiver if the child seems unusually sleepy or if she cannot wake him. Look to see if the child wakens when the caregiver talks to or shakes him, or when you clap your hands.

steps.title: LOOK: Is the child convulsing now?
steps.text: Look at the child. A child who is convulsing now has a general danger sign.

read.text: A breastfed child has a blocked nose and cannot suck. You clear his nose, and he breastfeeds well. Does he have the danger sign "not able to drink or breastfeed"?
read.answer: No. If the child can breastfeed after the nose is cleared, the child does not have the danger sign.

read.text: A child has vomited several times today, but he can hold down some fluids. Does he have the danger sign "vomits everything"?
read.answer: No. Only a child who cannot hold anything down at all has this sign.

read.text: What do you do if a child shows one or more general danger signs?

A child with a general danger sign has a serious problem. Most children with a general danger sign need urgent referral to hospital. The child might need lifesaving treatment with injectable antibiotics, oxygen, or other treatments that may not be available in your clinic.

If a child has a general danger sign, take IMMEDIATE ACTION: (1) complete the assessment immediately, because the child has a severe problem and there must be no delay in treatment; (2) provide urgent pre-referral treatment; (3) refer the child to hospital.
read.label: Immediate action

read.title: Does Lebo show any general danger signs?

stages.text: You ask if Lebo is able to drink or breastfeed, and Nthabeleng says, "No, not today, he is too tired." You try to give him some water from a cup but he is too weak and does not swallow. You ask Nthabeleng if Lebo is vomiting, and she says "no." You ask if Lebo is having convulsions, and Nthabeleng says "no."

You look at Lebo's condition. He is not paying attention to you or Nthabeleng as you talk, and only stares ahead. You snap your fingers in front of his face, but he does not look at the fingers. You ask Nthabeleng to bounce Lebo and speak to him, and when she says "Lebo! Lebo!" he does not look up at her.
stages.question: Which general danger signs does Lebo have?
options: Not able to drink, and lethargic
Vomits everything
No general danger sign
stages.explanation: Lebo is showing two general danger signs: he is unable to drink and he is lethargic. He needs to be referred immediately to the hospital.

stages.text: You tell Nthabeleng that Lebo needs further treatment at the hospital because he is unable to drink and is now acting very tired. You tell her it is very important that he go to the hospital right away, and that you will help arrange for her to get there. She looks very scared and asks if Lebo will die like his mother. She says this must be because of something she has done.
stages.question: What do you say to Nthabeleng?
options: Reassure her that it is because Lebo is sick, not because of her, and praise her for bringing him
Tell her there is nothing to worry about
Tell her she should have come sooner
stages.explanation: Affirm Nthabeleng: this is because Lebo is sick, not because of her actions. Explain that the treatment in the hospital will be able to help. Reassure her that she was a very good grandmother to bring Lebo, and very alert to notice that he was unwell.

stages.text: You tell her that you will start some immediate treatment now so that he can be stable during the journey to the hospital. You will then complete Lebo's assessment and decide what pre-referral treatment is necessary. He has a cough, so you must complete his classification for the cough to find the pre-referral treatment he needs. The lessons on urgent referral show you how.

read.text: How does the assessment continue after checking for general danger signs?

A child with any general danger sign needs URGENT attention. Complete the assessment and give any pre-referral treatment immediately so that referral is not delayed. You will learn much more about this in the following modules; your chart booklet walks you through the instructions.

read.title: What comes after the danger signs

cards.back: These are symptoms of the most common causes of illness and death in children under five: cough or difficult breathing (Module 3), diarrhoea (Module 4), and fever (Module 5). A number of illnesses, including pneumonia, malaria, or an infection, cause them.

Undernutrition is a very common underlying cause of child mortality. Even children with mild and moderate malnutrition have an increased risk of death. A sick child can be malnourished without you or the family noticing, and may have no complaints that point to malnutrition or anaemia. Module 6 covers this.

cards.front: Then: immunizations, HIV and other problems
cards.back: Modules 7, 8, 9 and additional modules explain these assessments.

read.text: Find the general danger signs in three children, and in a conversation with a mother.
read.label: In this lesson

dialogue.text: Good morning. What is the problem with your son today?
He has had a cough and fever for three days.
Is he able to drink or breastfeed?
Yes, he breastfeeds, but less than usual.

stages.question: What do you ask next?
options: Does he vomit everything?
Has he had his vaccines?
How many children do you have?
stages.explanation: Ask about each general danger sign in turn before anything else.
feedback: Right. Ask about each danger sign, one at a time.
Immunization is checked later, after assess and classify.
This is not part of checking for danger signs.

dialogue.text: No, he keeps the milk down.
Has he had convulsions during this illness?
Yes, yesterday evening he shook all over for a short time.

stages.question: What does this mean?
options: He has a general danger sign
It is only from the fever, so it does not count
Ask again tomorrow
stages.explanation: Convulsions during this illness are a general danger sign: the child needs urgent attention.
feedback: Right.
Convulsions in this illness count whatever the cause.
A child with a danger sign must not wait.

read.label: Test your skill
read.title: Does the child have a general danger sign?

cases.text: Huda's mother says Huda has vomited since this morning. When you ask, she says Huda vomits everything she eats or drinks, even water. Huda is awake and looks at you. She has had no convulsions.

record.title: Check for general danger signs
lines: Not able to drink or breastfeed: no

cases.question: Does Huda have a general danger sign?
options: Yes: she vomits everything
No: she is awake and alert
Not sure until you count her breaths
feedback: Right. A child who cannot keep anything down vomits everything. This is a general danger sign.
Being awake does not rule out a danger sign. Huda vomits everything, even water.
Breathing is part of the cough assessment. The danger signs are checked first, and Huda already has one.
cases.explanation: A child with any general danger sign needs URGENT attention: complete the assessment and any pre-referral treatment immediately, then refer.

cases.text: Adam has had fever for 2 days. His father says that last night Adam's arms and legs jerked and he did not respond for a few minutes. Now Adam is drinking and looks at you.
cases.question: Adam is drinking and alert now. Does he have a general danger sign?
options: No, because he is alert now
Yes: convulsions during this illness
Only if he convulses in the clinic
feedback: A convulsion during this illness is a general danger sign even if the child looks well now.
Right. Convulsions during the current illness are a general danger sign.
Convulsing now is one sign; a history of convulsions in this illness is another. Either one is a danger sign.
cases.explanation: Ask about convulsions in every sick child: "Has the child had convulsions during this illness?"

cases.text: Mai has a cough. She is sleeping on her mother's lap. When her mother speaks to her, she wakes, looks around and breastfeeds well. She has not vomited and has had no convulsions.

record.title: Check for general danger signs
lines: Lethargic or unconscious: no, wakes easily

cases.question: Is Mai lethargic?
options: Yes: she was asleep
No: she wakes easily and breastfeeds
Yes, because she has a cough
feedback: A sleeping child is not lethargic if she wakes when spoken to and looks around. Wake the child and look.
Right. A lethargic child is not alert when she should be and does not look at her mother. Mai wakes and feeds.
Cough is not a danger sign. Check each danger sign on its own.
cases.explanation: Mai has no general danger sign. Go on to assess her cough.

read.title: Care when urgent referral is required
read.caption: Watch this first. It walks through the whole section.

read.text: When is urgent referral required?

Children with general danger signs and/or any condition with a red classification require urgent pre-referral treatment and referral. These classifications indicate very serious illness. Look at the CLASSIFY table for general danger signs below: this is a red classification, and the treatments are in the TREAT column on the right.

read.caption: General danger signs (Sudan national IMNCI booklet)

read.text: Sudan national booklet: Two rows: "General danger sign: convulsing now" and "General danger sign present". The diazepam step adds airway care and a repeat dose after 10 minutes. No "keep the child warm" line. WHO module (page 18): One pink row, "Any general danger sign" classified as VERY SEVERE DISEASE: give diazepam if convulsing now; quickly complete the assessment; give any pre-referral treatment immediately; treat to prevent low blood sugar; keep the child warm; refer URGENTLY.
read.label: Sudan national protocol

read.text: Once you have identified a general danger sign, complete the IMCI assessment and determine any pre-referral treatment, so that you do not delay the referral.
read.label: Remember

read.text: How do you find the urgent pre-referral treatments?
Open your chart booklet. Where are the urgent pre-referral treatments?
read.answer: They are in bold print on the classification charts. For example, the DYSENTERY classification below shows ciprofloxacin as a pre-referral treatment.

read.text: Sudan national booklet: Ciprofloxacin for 3 days, zinc for 14 days, follow up in 3 days. WHO module (page 18): Give ciprofloxacin for 3 days; follow-up in 2 days (no zinc line).
read.label: Sudan national protocol

read.text: These are specified because some treatments should not be given before referral. Treatments that are not urgently needed will only delay referral.
Give it before referral, or not?

items.text: First dose of an antibiotic for severe pneumonia
items.why: It is in bold on the chart.

items.text: Treat the child to prevent low blood sugar
Teach the caregiver how to treat a local infection at home
items.why: Not urgent: it would only delay referral.
Not urgent: it would only delay referral.

items.text: Frequent sips of ORS on the way, for a child with dehydration and another severe classification

read.explanation: Only the treatments in bold are given before referral. Anything else only delays the referral.

read.text: Flip through your chart booklet
Look through each chart and find the pre-referral treatments in bold. Here are some examples of what you will see. You will learn more about these classifications in the coming modules.

Pre-referral treatments (Sudan national IMNCI booklet)

ClassificationPre-referral treatment identified
SEVERE PNEUMONIA or VERY SEVERE DISEASEFirst dose of antibiotic: oral amoxicillin if the child can take oral medicine; if the child cannot drink, vomits everything, is convulsing or lethargic, first dose of IM ampicillin and IM gentamicin. If wheezing, a rapid-acting inhaled bronchodilator. Treat to prevent low blood sugar
PNEUMONIAOral amoxicillin for 5 days (treated in the clinic)
SEVERE or SOME DEHYDRATION (with another severe classification)Refer urgently with the mother giving frequent sips of ORS on the way, and advise her to continue breastfeeding
VERY SEVERE FEBRILE DISEASEFirst dose of IM quinine; first dose of antibiotic (as for severe pneumonia); one dose of paracetamol for high fever (38.5 °C or above); treat to prevent low blood sugar
MALARIAArtemether-lumefantrine; one dose of paracetamol in clinic for high fever (38.5 °C or above)
COMPLICATED SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITIONFirst dose of antibiotic (as for severe pneumonia); treat to prevent low blood sugar; advise the mother to keep the child warm
SEVERE COMPLICATED MEASLES (and other measles classifications)Vitamin A treatment, and treatment of eye or mouth complications

Sudan national booklet: Rows use the Sudan names and treatments listed above. WHO module (page 19): WHO table (p. 19): SEVERE PNEUMONIA or VERY SEVERE DISEASE - first dose of an appropriate antibiotic, treat for low blood sugar. PNEUMONIA - first dose of oral amoxicillin. SEVERE or SOME DEHYDRATION (with another severe classification) - frequent sips of ORS on the way, continue breastfeeding. VERY SEVERE FEBRILE DISEASE - treatment for malaria if necessary, first doses of antibiotic and paracetamol for high fever. MEASLES - treatment for malaria if necessary, first dose of paracetamol for high fever. SEVERE ACUTE MALNUTRITION - low blood sugar, keep warm, first dose of antibiotic. Measles-related classifications - Vitamin A, and treatment if complications.

sections.title: How to refer a child urgently

read.text: Refer a child in four steps, and say what you do when referral is not possible.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: How do you urgently refer the child?
There are four steps to referring a child or a sick young infant to hospital.

steps.title: EXPLAIN the need for referral, and get her agreement
steps.text:
If you suspect that she does not want to take the child, find out why. Possible reasons:
  • She thinks hospitals are places where people often die, and fears her child will die there too.
  • She does not think that the hospital will help the child.
  • She cannot leave home and stay in the hospital: there is no one to take care of her other children, she is needed for farming, or she may lose a job.
  • She does not have money for transport, hospital bills, medicines, or food for herself during the stay.

steps.title: CALM her fears and help her resolve any problems
steps.text:
If she fears her child will die at the hospital, reassure her that the hospital has physicians, supplies, and equipment that can help cure her child.
  • Explain what will happen at the hospital and how that will help her child.
  • If she needs help at home while she is away, ask questions and make suggestions about who could help: for example, whether her husband, sister or another caregiver could help with the other children or with meals.
  • Discuss how she can travel to the hospital. Help arrange transport if necessary.
  • You may not be able to solve her problems and be sure that she goes, but it is important to do everything you can to help.

steps.title: WRITE A REFERRAL NOTE for her to carry
steps.text:
Tell her to give it to the health worker at the hospital. The note should include:
  • The name and age of the infant or child
  • The date and time of referral
  • Description of the child's problems
  • The reason for referral (signs and symptoms for the classification)
  • Treatment that you have given
  • Any other information the hospital needs to care for the child, such as earlier treatment of the illness or immunizations needed
  • Your name and the name of your clinic

steps.title: GIVE SUPPLIES AND INSTRUCTIONS for the way
steps.text:
If the hospital is far, give additional doses of antibiotic and tell her when to give them during the trip (by the dosage schedule on the TREAT chart). If you think she will not actually go to the hospital, give the full course of antibiotics and teach her how to give them.
  • Tell her how to keep the young child warm during the trip.
  • Advise her to continue breastfeeding.
  • If the child has some or severe dehydration and can drink, give her ORS solution for the child to sip frequently on the way.

read.text: Any child with a general danger sign or a serious classification requires urgent referral.
read.label: Remember

read.text: What if referral is not possible?

The best possible treatment for a child with a very severe illness is usually at a hospital. Sometimes referral is not possible or not advisable: the hospital may be too far, may not have adequate equipment or staff, or transport may not be available. Sometimes parents refuse to take a child to a hospital, in spite of the health worker's effort to explain the need for it.

If referral is not possible, do whatever you can to help the family care for the child. Continue pre-referral treatment until the child is able to leave for the hospital. If the child improves on pre-referral treatment, start treatment in the clinic (for example, the YELLOW classification). Advise the caregiver on all available treatment.

To help reduce deaths in severely ill children who cannot be referred, you may need to arrange for the child to stay in or near the clinic, where he may be seen several times a day. If not possible, arrange visits at home. There is more about this in the ANNEX.

stages.text: You have completed Lebo's assessment. You give him the urgent pre-referral treatments shown in bold on the classification charts where you classified his other conditions.
stages.question: Which of these goes in Lebo's referral note?
options: The treatment you have given him
Nthabeleng's household income
Nothing: the hospital will assess him again
stages.explanation: The referral note includes the name and age, date and time, the child's problems, the reason for referral, the treatment given, anything else the hospital needs to know, and your name and clinic.

stages.text: You prepare the referral note and give Nthabeleng the instructions for treatment on the way to the hospital. She is nervous, but you tell her that this treatment is urgent and should help Lebo, that she is taking very good care of him by being so alert and bringing him to the clinic herself, and that she is being a very good grandmother for taking him to the hospital.

sections.title: Using this module in your clinic

read.text: Plan how you will use what you learned in your own clinic.
read.label: In this lesson

read.text: Use your chart booklet and IMCI recording forms as you practise in the clinic. In the coming days, focus on the clinical skills below.

cards.back: Greet caregivers and use good communication skills to make them feel welcome in the clinic. Ask for important information from the caregiver: the child's name, age, problems, history, and so on.
Check all children for general danger signs. Use your chart booklet so that you ASK, LOOK, and FEEL for all signs. Record what you find on the IMCI recording form for sick children.
If the child has a general danger sign, classify as GENERAL DANGER SIGN PRESENT. If a child has a danger sign, practise preparing a caregiver for referral.

read.text: Remember to use your logbook

Now that you have completed the module, complete your logbook for MODULE 1:

  • Complete the Module 1 exercises.
  • Record at least 2 clinical cases from your clinic on the IMCI recording form, as you check children for general danger signs.
  • Take notes if you experience anything difficult, confusing, or interesting during these cases. They are valuable to share with your study group and at the face-to-face meeting.

Logbook checklist of clinical signs (sick child): tick each sign when you see it in a child at your clinic.

  • Not able to drink or breastfeed
  • Vomits everything
  • History of convulsions (with this illness)
  • Convulsions now
  • Lethargic or unconscious
Test what you have learned in Module 1.

Recap
read.text:
What you learned

  • Check every sick child for the general danger signs first.
  • Not able to drink or breastfeed, vomits everything, convulsions, lethargic or unconscious, convulsing now.
  • A child with any danger sign needs urgent attention and referral after pre-referral treatment.

In your clinic this week, record in your logbook three children you see for any illness, checking each one for the general danger signs: what you found, how you classified them and what you did. Bring the logbook to your next supervision visit or course session.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 1: Exercise C (Salina, 15 months)
narrative: Salina is 15 months old. She weighs 8.5 kg. Her temperature is 38.5 °C.
The health worker asked, "What are the child's problems?" The mother said, "Salina has been coughing for 4 days, and she is not eating well."
This is Salina's initial visit for this problem.
The health worker checked Salina for general danger signs. He asked, "Is Salina able to drink or breastfeed?" The mother said, "No. Salina does not want to breastfeed."
The health worker gave Salina some water. She was too weak to lift her head. She was not able to drink from a cup.
Next he asked the mother, "Is she vomiting?" The mother said, "No."
Then he asked, "Has she had convulsions?" The mother said, "No."
The health worker looked to see if Salina was lethargic or unconscious. When the health worker and the mother were talking, Salina watched them and looked around the room.
learningPoints: Salina was not able to drink from a cup, so she has the general danger sign "not able to drink or breastfeed".
She watched the health worker and her mother and looked around the room, so she is not lethargic.
One general danger sign is enough: the danger sign is present, and Salina needs urgent referral.
exercises.explain: Answer key: Module 1, page 25. Her problems: cough for 4 days, not eating well. Initial visit. Circle NOT ABLE TO DRINK OR BREASTFEED; danger sign present: Yes.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 1: Lebo, 19 months (the module case)
narrative: Lebo's grandmother carries him into the clinic. Lebo does not look well. She has walked for one hour to the clinic. She tells you that she is also taking care of 4 other grandchildren. Lebo is her youngest grandchild and she is very worried about him. She says he is acting very unwell and has had a cough for 7 days.

She tells you this is the first time she is bringing Lebo in to the clinic. You ask her how old Lebo is. She says he is 19 months old. You ask Lebo's grandmother her name. She tells you that her name is Nthabeleng.

What is Lebo's problem? Nthabeleng tells you that Lebo has had a cough for 7 days. She also says that he has not been eating well. Nthabeleng is very worried about this. She says that in the past two days, he cannot take anything at all and she says he is very weak. This is concerning to you.

Is Lebo coming for an initial or follow-up visit? Nthabeleng told you that this is her first time bringing him to the clinic for this issue. This is an initial visit. Lebo's temperature and weight were recorded when he came into the clinic, he weighs 10 kg and his temperature is 37 Celsius.

You ask if Lebo is able to drink or breastfeed, and Nthabeleng says, "no, not today, he is too tired." You try to give him some water from a cup but he is too weak and does not swallow. You ask Nthabeleng if Lebo is vomiting, and she says "no." You ask if Lebo is having convulsions, and Nthabeleng says "no."

You look at Lebo's condition. He is not paying attention to you or Nthabeleng as you talk, and only stares ahead. You snap your fingers in front of his face, but he does not look at the fingers. You ask Nthabeleng to bounce Lebo and speak to him, and when she says "Lebo! Lebo!" he does not look up at her.
learningPoints: Lebo is showing two general danger signs - he is unable to drink and lethargic. He needs to be referred immediately to the hospital.
exercises.explain: Lebo is showing two general danger signs - he is unable to drink and lethargic. He needs to be referred immediately to the hospital.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 1: Exercise D (true or false)

When you check your answers, the true version of each false statement is shown.

questions.question: Stop immediately and send the child to the hospital
questions.explain: The true statement: Continue the assessment quickly, identify all pre-referral treatments needed, treat, and refer urgently. Answer key: Module 1, page 25.

questions.question: Continue the assessment, determine pre-referral treatment, treat, and refer.
questions.explain: True. Answer key: Module 1, page 25.

questions.question: Continue to assess the child and send child to hospital with referral note about all of the treatments you identified.
questions.explain: The true statement: You should deliver the necessary pre-referral treatment before they leave your clinic for the hospital. Answer key: Module 1, page 25.

questions.question: If referral is not possible, there is nothing you can do. Send the child home.
questions.explain: The true statement: You can provide essential care (further discussed in Annex), work with the family to encourage them to go to the hospital, or bring the child near to the clinic to monitor treatment and progress. Answer key: Module 1, page 25.

exercises.title: Distance learning Module 1: Logbook test
narrative: Below are questions about the module. You are allowed to use your Chart Booklet as you answer these questions. You should not use your study modules.

questions.question: According to IMCI charts, a sick child is:
options: Under two months of age
Under 5 years of age
2 months up to 5 years of age
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: What is the first thing you do when a caregiver and child enter your clinic room?
options: Take the child and examine him
Greet the caregiver to make her feel welcome
Give the child treatment
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: Sami is 2 months old. Sami is a:
options: A sick young infant
A sick child
Neither
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: What important information do you need about the child before you begin your assessment?
options: If the child has general danger signs
Age, weight, temperature, child's problem according to caregiver, and if the visit is initial or follow-up
Why the caregiver came to the clinic
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: What is a general danger sign?
options: A sign that a sick young infant is ill
A sign that the child is beginning to get sick, so the mother should watch him more carefully at home
A sign of very serious illness in a sick child, which requires urgent referral
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: Which of the following is a general danger sign in sick children?
options: Vomiting frequently
Fast breathing
Unable to breastfeed, eat, or drink
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: How do you check if a child is unable to breastfeed or drink?
options: You can tell by looking because the child will be small
Ask the caregiver to give a drink or clean water or breast milk. See if the child will take the liquid into his mouth and swallow it.
Look at the child's lips to see if they are dry
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: How would you explain "convulsions" to a caregiver?
options: The child's arms and legs stiffen, and he might lose consciousness.
The child will fall on the floor and his body will shake violently.
The child's face muscles will twitch.
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: How will you determine if a child is vomiting everything?
options: Ask if the child has been vomiting frequently.
Ask the caregiver if the child has vomited everything that they swallowed or drank. If they are unsure, give the child something to drink and see if they vomit.
Ask if the child has vomited at least 5 times in the past 24 hours, because the frequency of vomiting determines this sign.
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: If a child is lethargic, how does he look and act?
options: He is drowsy and is not alert or awake. He will not show interest in what is happening around him, he only stares ahead.
His eyes are closed, and he appears unconscious.
He will respond once you speak or clap.
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: If a child is unconscious, how does he look and act?
options: His eyes follow your hand if you wave in front of his face.
He acts very sleepy.
He will not wake, even when someone shakes him. His eyes could be closed or open. If they are open, they do not follow any objects.
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: If a child has a general danger sign, what are the steps taken?
options: Stop everything and send the child to the hospital.
Complete the IMCI assessment without delay so that you can determine if the child has any other critical health issues. Identify and give pre-referral treatments, and prepare a referral note.
Counsel the mother on home treatment and feeding
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: If a child has a severe (RED) classification and needs to be urgently referred, how do you determine the pre-referral treatment?
options: Use your best guess to decide on a treatment for whatever is causing the severe illness
No pre-referral treatment needed, send the child immediately to the hospital to not delay.
Pre-referral treatments are listed in bold type in the classification tables. Give all pre-referral treatments for all classifications.
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: Important pre-referral treatments include:
options: Treating low blood sugar
Breastfeeding assessments and counselling for feeding problems
Oral rehydration therapy in the clinic
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: Only children who are unconscious require urgent referral.

questions.question: A child whose nose is blocked may have trouble breastfeeding. You must clear the nose to check if the child is able to drink.

questions.question: If a child has a general danger sign, stop the assessment immediately and send them to the hospital.
questions.explain: Answer key: Facilitator guide, Annex A3.2.

questions.question: If referral is not possible, there is not much you can do, so you should send the child home.
